summary:
The Republic of Mordovia stands under the national framework of the Russia Federation, which applies in full and without identified local deviation; the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, June 2025) assesses the territory at the national score and records no regional departure.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage is prohibited and gender transition is banned. Legal gender recognition and gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, when the law barring gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to documents took effect. Visitors whose documents carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation have no domestic route to correct it.

The expanded propaganda statute criminalises public expression that explicitly includes anything justifying gender transition. The 2013 "gay propaganda" law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation, and national government warnings directed at LGBT travellers state this plainly.

Since the 2023 Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, participation carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising carries six to ten years. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 of them administrative and three criminal, for alleged participation in that movement or for displaying its symbols. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect them. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims; Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Enforcement has grown in volume as well as severity: Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws had increased eighteenfold over the previous decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, with a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that "Ada", a transgender woman, was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
tangentialFactors:
Russia's framework punishes expression rather than same-sex conduct itself: consensual same-sex activity remains lawful while public display, advocacy and any communication framed as justifying gender transition attract fines, detention or imprisonment. The asymmetry matters for a visitor because ordinary conduct such as a social media post or a visible symbol can supply the evidentiary basis for an administrative or criminal case.

Enforcement is escalating measurably. Human Rights Watch counted 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, and Meduza recorded an eighteenfold rise in propaganda-law cases over a decade alongside more than 60 million rubles in collected fines, indicating a functioning enforcement apparatus rather than an unused statute.

Organised venues and intermediaries are targeted alongside individuals. The raids on Moscow bars in January 2024, the extremism charges against staff of a publishing house, and the death in pretrial detention of a man held over an LGBTQ+ travel agency each show that association with queer spaces carries its own exposure.

The UK asylum standard treats LGBT+ Russians, including those from the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as members of a particular social group under the refugee convention, and Human Rights Watch has asked governments to offer safe haven. This is relevant to onward travel planning for anyone leaving Russia rather than entering it.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Republic of Mordovia have no legal means of changing gender markers on Russian documents and no lawful access to gender-affirming healthcare, both prohibited under the national framework in force since 2023.

Domestic participation in, or display of symbols associated with, the designated "international LGBT movement" carries two to six years' imprisonment, and organising carries six to ten years. Administrative liability under article 20.3 applies to displaying banned symbols and has produced the bulk of the convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch.

The UK Home Office assessed at least 139 people across Russia as impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and concluded that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution while the state is able but unwilling to protect them. Protection machinery therefore exists on paper without being applied in practice.

Coercive conversion practices are documented in Russia: BBC Russian described a transgender woman held for nine months at a centre near Novosibirsk from summer 2021, forced to take testosterone and to perform manual labour until she escaped.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement of the propaganda statutes, extremism designations or anti-trans provisions by courts or police within the Republic of Mordovia itself; the enforcement figures cited are national. Whether Mordovia's own courts have processed such cases is unresolved.

Entry, visa and border-screening procedures applicable to transgender travellers arriving in Russia are not addressed by the inventory beyond the general penalty exposure for foreigners, including deportation. Document inspection practice at points of entry remains not sourced.

The counts from Human Rights Watch are stated as of 30 June 2025 and the UK Home Office note reflects material to June 2025 with a later page update; later totals are not sourced here.

The inventory does not state whether the banned procedures were withdrawn or merely suspended in practice, nor whether any clinical exceptions persist; "effectively banned" is the wording used by the UK Home Office note.
